reading.sentence: Across 60 rows and 496 numeric columns, measured on a log scale, the column means spread 8 times as widely as the row means, which is what one row per sample looks like.

lens_hints.because: 496 columns hold non-negative whole numbers whose mean counts span 1.1 orders of magnitude across the middle half of them, as genes' do

base.basis: Column summaries and lens hints read all 60 rows.

if_one_row.message: `gene_0153` has 28 distinct values across 60 rows, about 2.14 each. That is the shape of repeated measures, and you answered one row per person. One of those two readings is wrong, and which one changes how the held-out rows are chosen.

findings.title: `486` columns hold raw counts, and library sizes differ by sample.
findings.detail: `486` columns are whole numbers from 0 to `26,471`. Each sample's total over them, its library size, runs from `19,553` to `60,376`, a 3.1-fold spread. On raw counts a sample sequenced deeper has larger values in every gene.
findings.why_it_matters: A model fit to raw counts can read sequencing depth as biology: in a test with no gene differing, cases sequenced 1.46 times deeper gave a cross-validated AUC near 1. Linear models wait until a normalization is chosen or you state the values are already normalized.
findings.summary: `486` columns are raw counts; library sizes vary 3.1-fold, so depth would read as biology.

repairs.label: Log-CPM with TMM
repairs.consequence: TMM factors from each training fold scale library sizes; values become log2 counts per million.
repairs.sentence: Of the 486 count columns, those of them the models take as exposures were transformed to log2 counts per million (edgeR cpm, prior count 2) on library sizes scaled by TMM factors (Robinson and Oshlack 2010), fit within each training fold.

repairs.label: Log-CPM, library size only
repairs.consequence: Each sample's own library size divides its counts, then log2; no TMM composition factors.
repairs.sentence: Of the 486 count columns, those of them the models take as exposures were transformed to log2 counts per million (edgeR cpm, prior count 2) on each sample's library size, the mean library size taken within each training fold.

findings.title: 496 count columns against 60 samples.
findings.detail: Every value in them is a non-negative integer, p/n is 8.3, and total depth per sample varies 3.1-fold.
findings.why_it_matters: Two consequences, and only one of them is ours to settle. Model ranking is: at this p/n an unregularized fit is not merely optimistic but degenerate, so regularized models rank first and distance-based ones last — ordered, never filtered. Normalization is NOT: CPM, TPM and VST answer different questions and are not interchangeable, and the right one depends on the assay and on what you are asking. No normalization default is asserted here, and that is the considered position rather than an omission.
findings.summary: `496` count columns against `60` samples: an unpenalized model has no unique fit.

findings.title: `batch` groups rows.
findings.detail: `batch` has `3` values across `60` rows, at most `20` rows each. It groups participants rather than naming them.
findings.why_it_matters: Rows that share a site or household share whatever differs between sites or households, so intervals that treat them as independent are too narrow.
findings.summary: `batch` groups `60` rows into `3` clusters, such as sites or households; rows within one are not independent.

findings.title: `condition` is a binary variable written as text.
findings.detail: `condition` holds two values — 'control' (30 rows) and 'case' (30 rows). It is a binary variable, not a number stored as text.
findings.why_it_matters: Read as binary, control becomes 1 and case becomes 0. Which level is the positive one is your call — nothing in the file says — and the direction of every coefficient for this variable follows from it.
findings.summary: `condition` is two-level text (`case`, `control`); which level counts as 1 is not asked yet.

findings.title: What your numbers are: Raw counts.
findings.detail: 496 columns across 60 samples. Every value is a whole number and the matrix reaches well past ten thousand. Nothing else in the table reads that way.
findings.why_it_matters: Raw counts keep what a count model needs: DESeq2 and edgeR estimate measurement precision from them and correct for library size themselves, so a count model takes the counts as they are. The models in this app read the values directly, so here the counts need a normalization first. For inference, the feature-wise tests run on log counts per million with TMM factors, one linear model per gene as limma fits, without its variance moderation. For prediction, the same normalization is refit within each training fold. Whether to normalize matters far more than where: for microarray data, Hornung and colleagues (2015) found that normalizing the whole table before cross-validation "did not result in a noteworthy optimistic bias".

evidence.source: research/GENOMICS_PACK.md#02 · Data-type detection — the highest-leverage diagnostic in the pack

findings.summary: What your numbers are: Raw counts. No control for this yet.

findings.title: `sample_id` names each row.
findings.detail: `sample_id` has `60` different values across `60` rows, one per row. A value that appears once cannot tell a model anything about a row it has not seen.
findings.why_it_matters: As a predictor it would be noise at best, and a way to memorize rows at worst.
findings.summary: `sample_id` is unique on every row: it names its row and is not a predictor.

findings.title: `gene_0049` holds low counts, not missing-value codes.
findings.detail:
Found 7 (3×): above every other value (the largest is 4), past an unused value at the top of a coded question whose top answer is common, which is where a scale ends and its codes begin. These are conventional codes for a missing answer, and nothing in the numbers separates a code from a real extreme value, so the reading is a proposal.

This is a count column, and a small integer in a low-expression gene is a count rather than a missing-value code. The detector reads an integral column with few distinct values as a coded variable, which is the right reading for a survey item and the wrong one for a transcript count.
findings.why_it_matters: Survey and clinical exports code missing answers as 999, -9, or 7/8/9 in coded questions. Left as numbers they are averaged into your results; recoded wrongly, they remove real extreme values.
findings.summary: `gene_0049` holds low counts: `7` is a count, not a missing-value code; nothing needs repairing.

findings.title: The wide shape is expected here.
findings.detail:
gene_00 (99: gene_0001, gene_0002, gene_0003…); gene_01 (100: gene_0100, gene_0101, gene_0102…); gene_02 (100: gene_0200, gene_0201, gene_0202…).

These are different genes, not one gene measured several times. Reshaping to long format would rebuild what a row is.
findings.why_it_matters: Wide repeated measures are fine for prediction, but if each row is a subject measured several times you may want one row per measurement instead — and clustered rows need a group-aware split.
findings.summary: The wide shape is expected for this kind of data; nothing needs changing.

models.label: Elastic net

versus_baseline.tolerance_basis: Better only when the gain's 95% interval lies above zero and the gain is at least 0.01 (a convention): a gain above 0.056. The interval is corrected for the 50 folds sharing training rows (Nadeau & Bengio 2003).

calibration.smoother: lowess, span 2/3, no robustness iterations (as rms val.prob)

models.performance: Cross-validated log loss 0.150 (95% interval 0.096 to 0.205, likely too narrow (Bates, Hastie & Tibshirani 2023): 497 candidate predictors for 48 rows (p/n 10.4, above the 1 this app takes as p ≫ n)) by 5-fold cross-validation: the expected performance of this modeling procedure at this sample size.
models.methods: Within each training fold, log-CPM with TMM factors and autoscaling were fitted and applied to the held-out fold; elastic-net parameters were tuned in an inner CV nested in an outer CV.

base.cv_definition: Cross-validated scores are the mean over folds; the fold values show the spread.
base.se_definition: Each standard error counts which rows were scored, with each fold's model as fitted (LeDell et al. 2015; DeLong's for the AUC); it leaves out how the models would vary with other training rows.
base.precision: On these 48 training rows the cross-validated log loss has a standard error of 0.028 for Elastic net; whether two families differ is read from their paired interval, not from either one alone.
base.imbalance: The event, `case`, is 50% of the training rows. No resampling (SMOTE, over- or undersampling) or class weighting was applied: customary in machine-learning papers, resampling overestimates the rarer class's probability without raising the AUC (van den Goorbergh et al. 2022); a decision moves the threshold instead.
base.tension: AUC is the customary headline: it ranks risks without asking whether they are right (semi-proper), so the models were compared, chosen and declared on log loss, a strictly proper score (Van Calster et al., STRATOS TG6).

comparison.method: the corrected repeated k-fold t (Nadeau & Bengio 2003; Bouckaert & Frank 2004)

result.sentence: The held-out rows score the final model, declared on cross-validation before they are opened; its held-out log loss will be the result.
